input: Learn to read a mutual fund prospectus properly

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: A prospectus has many sections — fees, risk factors, performance history, fund strategy, management, tax info. Knowing which sections matter most to this user determines how deep and broad the plan needs to be.
Whether this is for personal investing, helping a family member, or a professional/academic purpose changes the depth, tone, and framing of the learning plan entirely.

Whether the user already has a specific prospectus in hand (e.g. for a fund they are considering) vs. learning generically changes whether the plan should be abstract or hands-on with a real document.
How much time the user can dedicate determines whether this is a quick focused session or a multi-week structured learning effort.
Some people learn best through guided reading, others through videos, summaries, or worked examples. The preferred learning style shapes what resources and methods to recommend.
The user's definition of 'properly' is critical — it could mean spotting red flags, comparing two funds, understanding fee drag, or being able to explain it to someone else.
Knowing the user's current financial literacy baseline avoids over-explaining basics to an experienced investor or skipping essential groundwork for a beginner.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to read a mutual fund prospectus properly
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to develop the skill of reading and understanding a mutual fund prospectus, likely to make more informed investment decisions.

questions.title: Which sections of a prospectus matter most to you?
questions.description: Find out whether the user wants to focus on specific parts — such as fees and expenses, risk factors, fund strategy, or performance history — or get a complete end-to-end understanding of the whole document.

questions.title: Is this for your own investing or another purpose?
questions.description: Determine whether the user is learning for personal investment decisions, to assist a family member or friend, for a work or academic requirement, or some other reason, as this shapes the depth and framing of the plan.

questions.title: Do you have a specific prospectus you are working with?
questions.description: Establish whether the user has a real fund document in hand they want to decode, or whether they want to learn the skill in a general, fund-agnostic way.

questions.title: How much time can you set aside for this?
questions.description: Clarify the user's available time commitment — a single focused session, a few hours over a week, or a longer structured effort — so the plan can be scoped and paced appropriately.

questions.title: How do you learn best — reading, videos, or worked examples?
questions.description: Understand the user's preferred learning format so the right mix of resources, exercises, and methods can be recommended — whether that is annotated readings, YouTube explainers, side-by-side comparisons, or something else.

questions.title: What would reading a prospectus 'properly' look like for you?
questions.description: Pin down the user's concrete success criteria — for example, being able to compare two funds confidently, spot hidden fees, identify unsuitable risk levels, or explain the fund to someone else.

questions.title: How familiar are you with basic investing concepts already?
questions.description: Gauge the user's current financial literacy baseline — complete beginner, some familiarity with stocks and funds, or experienced investor — so the plan does not over-explain or skip essential groundwork.
